title: Fixed-Priority Schedulability of Sporadic Tasks on Uniprocessors is NP-Hard

extraction.paper_name: Fixed-Priority Schedulability of Sporadic Tasks on Uniprocessors is NP-hard
extraction.paper_description: This paper investigates the computational complexity of the Fixed-Priority (FP) schedulability problem for sporadic or synchronous periodic tasks on a preemptive uniprocessor. It demonstrates that this problem is (weakly) NP-hard, even under specific restrictions such as implicit deadlines with Rate-Monotonic (RM) priority ordering, or constrained deadlines with Deadline-Monotonic (DM) priority ordering and bounded utilization. The proof relies on a series of reductions from the known coNP-complete EDF-schedulability problem.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic task tau is represented as a triple (e, d, p) of positive integers.

variables.p: period (minimum separation time between consecutive job releases)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the parameters of a sporadic task.

informal_sketch.intuition: A sporadic task is a recurring activity in a real-time system, characterized by how long it takes to execute, when it needs to finish, and how often it can be released.
steps: e: The maximum time the task needs on the CPU.
d: The time interval from a job's release by which it must complete.
p: The minimum time between the release of two consecutive jobs of this task.
key_insights: This model captures the essential timing requirements for real-time tasks.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is a (multi-)set of tasks.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a collection of tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task set is simply a group of individual tasks that need to be scheduled together on a processor.
steps: Collect multiple SporadicTask objects into a list or set.
informal_sketch.pseudocode: task_set = [SporadicTask(10, 20, 50), SporadicTask(5, 15, 30)]
key_insights: The interaction and interference between tasks in a set are central to schedulability analysis.

formal_description.statement: A task set T has implicit deadlines if d = p for all (e, d, p) in T.
assumptions: All tasks in T are sporadic tasks (Definition 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Characterizes a task set where deadlines are equal to periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: In an implicit deadline system, a task must complete its execution before its next job can be released. This simplifies analysis.
steps: For every task in the set, check if its relative deadline (d) is exactly equal to its period (p).
If this holds for all tasks, the set has implicit deadlines.
key_insights: This is the simplest deadline model, often used for initial theoretical analysis.

formal_description.statement: A task set T has constrained deadlines if d <= p for all (e, d, p) in T.
assumptions: All tasks in T are sporadic tasks (Definition 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Characterizes a task set where deadlines are less than or equal to periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: In a constrained deadline system, a task must complete its execution before its next job is released, or at the very latest, at the same time its next job is released. This is a common and practical model.
steps: For every task in the set, check if its relative deadline (d) is less than or equal to its period (p).
If this holds for all tasks, the set has constrained deadlines.
key_insights: This model is more general than implicit deadlines but still avoids the complexities of jobs having deadlines after subsequent jobs are released.

formal_description.statement: A task set T has arbitrary deadlines if no restrictions are placed on the relation between d and p.
assumptions: All tasks in T are sporadic tasks (Definition 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Characterizes a task set where deadlines can be less than, equal to, or greater than periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the most general deadline model, where a task's deadline can occur after its next job is released. This makes schedulability analysis significantly more complex.
steps: No specific check is needed; if a task set doesn't fit implicit or constrained deadlines, it has arbitrary deadlines.
key_insights: This model is the most flexible but also the most challenging for schedulability analysis.

formal_description.statement: The Fixed-Priority (FP) scheduling algorithm takes a fixed (total) priority ordering of the tasks in the task set and then executes jobs strictly according to this priority ordering. At any time point, it chooses among the ready jobs to execute the job with the highest priority, preempting any lower-priority job if needed. If several jobs from the same task are ready, these are prioritized in FIFO order.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines how tasks are scheduled under Fixed-Priority scheduling.

informal_sketch.intuition: FP scheduling assigns a static priority to each task. The CPU always runs the highest-priority task that is ready to execute. If a higher-priority task becomes ready, it can interrupt a lower-priority task.
steps: Assign a unique, fixed priority to each task.
Maintain a queue of ready jobs, ordered by task priority (highest first).
If multiple jobs from the same task are ready, use FIFO (first-in, first-out) order.
At any time, execute the highest-priority job in the ready queue.
If a new job arrives with higher priority than the currently executing job, preempt the current job and run the new one.
key_insights: Simplicity and efficiency of implementation are key advantages of FP scheduling.

formal_description.statement: The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm chooses among the ready jobs to execute the job with the earliest absolute deadline (ties broken arbitrarily), preempting a job with a later deadline if needed.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines how tasks are scheduled under Earliest Deadline First scheduling.

informal_sketch.intuition: EDF scheduling prioritizes jobs dynamically based on their absolute deadlines. The job that needs to finish soonest gets the CPU. This is known to be an optimal uniprocessor scheduler.
steps: Maintain a queue of ready jobs, ordered by their absolute deadlines (earliest first).
If multiple jobs have the same absolute deadline, break ties arbitrarily.
At any time, execute the job with the earliest absolute deadline.
If a new job arrives with an earlier absolute deadline than the currently executing job, preempt the current job and run the new one.
key_insights: EDF is optimal on uniprocessors, meaning if any scheduler can schedule a task set, EDF can.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is FP-schedulable with a given priority ordering if and only if all jobs generated by T will always complete execution by their deadlines when using the FP scheduler with that priority ordering on a preemptive uniprocessor.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines what it means for a task set to be schedulable under FP.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task set is FP-schedulable if, no matter when jobs are released (within their minimum separation times), all jobs always finish before their deadlines when using a specific fixed-priority scheme.
steps: Simulate or analyze the FP scheduling of the task set with a given priority order.
If, for all possible job release scenarios, every job completes its execution by its absolute deadline, then the task set is FP-schedulable.
key_insights: Schedulability means meeting all deadlines under all valid release patterns.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is EDF-schedulable if and only if all jobs generated by T will always complete execution by their deadlines when using the EDF scheduler on a preemptive uniprocessor.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines what it means for a task set to be schedulable under EDF.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task set is EDF-schedulable if, no matter when jobs are released (within their minimum separation times), all jobs always finish before their deadlines when using EDF scheduling.
steps: Simulate or analyze the EDF scheduling of the task set.
If, for all possible job release scenarios, every job completes its execution by its absolute deadline, then the task set is EDF-schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_edf_schedulable(task_set):
    # This is a complex analysis, often involving demand bound functions
    # Check if U_T <= 1 and dbf_T_lambda <= lambda for all relevant lambda
    U_T = calculate_utilization(task_set)
    if U_T > 1:
        return False
    # Further checks using dbf_T_lambda
    return True # Simplified for sketch
key_insights: EDF schedulability is a fundamental concept, often used as a baseline due to its optimality.

formal_description.statement: A synchronous periodic task is defined by a triple (e, d, p) of positive integers, where p denotes the exact separation between consecutive job releases, and the first job of all such tasks are released synchronously at the same time point.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the parameters of a synchronous periodic task.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a more rigid task model than sporadic. Jobs are released at precise, regular intervals, and all tasks start at the same time. This simplifies analysis by removing release jitter.
steps: e: The maximum time the task needs on the CPU.
d: The time interval from a job's release by which it must complete.
p: The exact time between the release of two consecutive jobs of this task.
All tasks' first jobs are released at time 0.
key_insights: This model is often used for worst-case analysis because synchronous releases can create peak demand.

formal_description.statement: The priority ordering that assigns higher priority to tasks with shorter relative deadlines (ties broken arbitrarily) is known as the Deadline-Monotonic (DM) priority ordering.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific priority assignment policy.

informal_sketch.intuition: DM priority assignment is a heuristic where tasks with tighter deadlines are given higher priority. The idea is that tasks that need to finish sooner should get preferential treatment.
steps: For each task, identify its relative deadline (d).
Sort tasks in ascending order of their relative deadlines.
Assign higher priorities to tasks appearing earlier in the sorted list (i.e., shorter deadlines get higher priority).
If two tasks have the same deadline, their relative priority can be arbitrary.
key_insights: DM is optimal for constrained-deadline task sets under FP scheduling.

formal_description.statement: The Rate-Monotonic (RM) priority ordering assigns higher priority to tasks with shorter periods.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines another specific priority assignment policy.

informal_sketch.intuition: RM priority assignment gives higher priority to tasks that arrive more frequently (i.e., have shorter periods). The rationale is that more frequent tasks need to be serviced more often.
steps: For each task, identify its period (p).
Sort tasks in ascending order of their periods.
Assign higher priorities to tasks appearing earlier in the sorted list (i.e., shorter periods get higher priority).
If two tasks have the same period, their relative priority can be arbitrary.
key_insights: RM is optimal for implicit-deadline task sets under FP scheduling. For implicit deadlines, RM is equivalent to DM.

formal_description.statement: U_T def = sum((e_i, d_i, p_i) in T) e_i / p_i

variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: Tasks are sporadic or synchronous periodic (Definition 1 or 10).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total processor utilization of a task set.

informal_sketch.intuition: Utilization represents the fraction of processor time that the task set requires. If utilization is greater than 1, the task set is definitely unschedulable on a single processor.
steps: For each task, calculate its individual utilization: e_i / p_i.
Sum these individual utilizations for all tasks in the set.
key_insights: Utilization is a fundamental metric for schedulability. It provides a necessary condition (U_T <= 1) for schedulability.

formal_description.statement: rbf_T_r def = sum((e_i, d_i, p_i) in T) ceil(r / p_i) * e_i

variables.rbf_T_r: request bound function of task set T in interval r
variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: Tasks are sporadic or synchronous periodic (Definition 1 or 10).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum cumulative execution time requested by tasks in T within any interval of length r, assuming all tasks are released at the start of the interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: The request bound function calculates the maximum amount of CPU time that a set of tasks (or a subset, like higher-priority tasks) could demand within a given time window 'r'. This is crucial for calculating response times.
steps: For each task tau_i in the set T:
Calculate the maximum number of jobs of tau_i that could be released and demand execution within an interval of length 'r'. This is ceil(r / p_i).
Multiply this by the task's execution time e_i.
Sum these values for all tasks in T.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def rbf(task_set, r):
    total_request = 0
    for task in task_set:
        # Number of jobs that could be released in interval r
        num_jobs = math.ceil(r / task.p)
        total_request += num_jobs * task.e
    return total_request
key_insights: This function quantifies the interference a task can experience from higher-priority tasks, which is central to response time analysis.

formal_description.statement: dbf_T_lambda def = sum((e_i, d_i, p_i) in T) max(0, floor((lambda - d_i) / p_i) + 1) * e_i. For a task set T with constrained deadlines, this simplifies to: dbf_T_lambda = sum((e_i, d_i, p_i) in T) (floor((lambda - d_i) / p_i) + 1) * e_i.

variables.dbf_T_lambda: demand bound function of task set T in interval length lambda
variables.e_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: Tasks are sporadic or synchronous periodic (Definition 1 or 10).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum cumulative execution time demanded by jobs of tasks in T that are released at or before time 0 and have deadlines at or before lambda.

informal_sketch.intuition: The demand bound function calculates the maximum amount of CPU time that a task set *demands* to complete jobs whose deadlines fall within a specific interval `lambda`. This is used to check if the processor can keep up with the workload.
steps: For each task tau_i in the set T:
Calculate the number of jobs of tau_i whose deadlines fall within the interval `[0, lambda]`. This is `floor((lambda - d_i) / p_i) + 1` (assuming first job at time 0).
Ensure this count is non-negative (using `max(0, ...)`)
Multiply this count by the task's execution time e_i.
Sum these values for all tasks in T.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def dbf(task_set, lambda_val):
    total_demand = 0
    for task in task_set:
        # Number of jobs whose deadlines are within lambda_val
        num_jobs = math.floor((lambda_val - task.d) / task.p) + 1
        total_demand += max(0, num_jobs) * task.e
    return total_demand
key_insights: dbf is a key tool for EDF schedulability analysis, ensuring that the total demand does not exceed the available time.

formal_description.statement: P_T def = lcm{p_i | (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T}
assumptions: Tasks are sporadic or synchronous periodic (Definition 1 or 10).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the least common multiple of all task periods in a task set.

informal_sketch.intuition: The hyper-period is the shortest time interval after which the pattern of job releases for all tasks in the set repeats. It's a critical interval for schedulability analysis because if a system is schedulable over one hyper-period, it's schedulable indefinitely.
steps: Collect all unique periods (p_i) from the tasks in T.
Calculate the least common multiple (LCM) of these periods.
key_insights: Schedulability only needs to be checked over the interval [0, P_T) for many scheduling algorithms.

formal_description.statement: g_n is the smallest number such that all intervals of g_n consecutive integers a, a+1, ..., a+g_n-1 contain at least one number that is coprime to n. An upper bound is g_n <= K * log_2(n) for n >= 2 and some unknown positive constant K.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a number-theoretic function related to the distribution of coprime numbers.

informal_sketch.intuition: The Jacobsthal function tells us how large an interval of integers we need to guarantee finding a number that shares no common factors (other than 1) with a given number 'n'. This is used in the paper to ensure that task periods can be made pairwise coprime.
steps: Given an integer 'n', find the smallest 'g_n' such that any sequence of 'g_n' consecutive integers will contain at least one integer 'x' where `gcd(x, n) == 1`.
The paper uses an upper bound for 'g_n' to show that such coprime numbers can be found within a polynomially bounded range.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_coprime(a, b):
    import math
    return math.gcd(a, b) == 1

def jacobsthal_function(n):
    # This is a complex number theory function, not easily computable directly
    # The paper uses its properties and bounds, not direct computation.
    # For example, to find a number coprime to N in an interval [start, start + g(N) - 1]:
    # for x in range(start, start + g_n_upper_bound):
    #     if is_coprime(x, n):
    #         return x
    pass
key_insights: This function guarantees the existence of coprime numbers within certain intervals, which is crucial for constructing task sets with specific period properties.

formal_description.statement: n_T_c def = |T_c|

variables.n_T_c: number of tasks in task set T_c

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the count of tasks in a specific task set T_c.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is simply the total number of tasks in the input task set `T_c` for the reduction.
steps: Count the elements in the task set `T_c`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def get_num_tasks(task_set_c):
    return len(task_set_c)
key_insights: Used as a parameter in scaling factors and bounds.

formal_description.statement: kappa def = (10 * K * n_T_c * P_T_c)_power_3
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a large scaling factor used in the reduction from EDF-schedulability to FP-schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: Kappa is a very large number derived from the properties of the input task set. It's used to scale task parameters (execution times, deadlines, periods) to ensure certain mathematical properties hold for the reduction, particularly to make periods large enough to find coprime values.
steps: Calculate the hyper-period `P_T_c` of the input task set `T_c`.
Get the number of tasks `n_T_c`.
Multiply `10 * K * n_T_c * P_T_c`.
Raise this product to the power of 3.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_kappa(K_const, n_T_c, P_T_c):
    return (10 * K_const * n_T_c * P_T_c)**3
key_insights: This large scaling factor is crucial for the number-theoretic properties required in the reduction, ensuring that period adjustments for coprimality do not significantly alter schedulability behavior.

results.identifier: Definition 20: T_perp_c and its task parameters

formal_description.statement: T_perp_c def = {(e_i_prime, d_i_prime, p_i_prime) | (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T_c}, where e_i_prime def = kappa * e_i, d_i_prime def = kappa * d_i, and p_i_prime def = min{m * kappa * p_i | m is coprime to p_j_prime, forall j < i}. Tasks in T_c are indexed by non-decreasing periods, so p_j <= p_i if j < i.

variables.T_perp_c: transformed task set with pairwise coprime periods
variables.e_i_prime: scaled execution time of task i
variables.d_i_prime: scaled relative deadline of task i
variables.p_i_prime: scaled and adjusted period of task i
variables.e_i: original execution time of task i
variables.d_i: original relative deadline of task i

assumptions: T_c is a task set with constrained deadlines and utilization bounded by c (0 < c < 1).
Tasks in T_c are ordered by non-decreasing periods.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a new task set T_perp_c where task parameters are scaled by kappa, and periods are further adjusted to be pairwise coprime, while preserving constrained deadlines and utilization bounds.

informal_sketch.intuition: This definition describes how to transform an input task set `T_c` into a new task set `T_perp_c` that has two key properties: all task parameters are scaled up by `kappa`, and critically, all task periods are made pairwise coprime (meaning no two periods share a common factor other than 1). This coprimality is essential for the duality argument in the second reduction step.
steps: For each task `tau_i = (e_i, d_i, p_i)` in `T_c` (ordered by non-decreasing periods):
Calculate `e_i_prime = kappa * e_i`.
Calculate `d_i_prime = kappa * d_i`.
Find the smallest integer `m` such that `m * kappa * p_i` is coprime to all previously determined `p_j_prime` (for `j < i`).
Set `p_i_prime = m * kappa * p_i`.
The new task `tau_i_prime = (e_i_prime, d_i_prime, p_i_prime)` is added to `T_perp_c`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
import math

def is_coprime(a, b):
    return math.gcd(a, b) == 1

def create_T_perp_c(T_c, kappa):
    T_perp_c = []
    # Assume T_c is already sorted by period
    for i, task in enumerate(T_c):
        e_i_prime = kappa * task.e
        d_i_prime = kappa * task.d

        # Find p_i_prime
        current_p_val = kappa * task.p
        m = 1
        while True:
            candidate_p_i_prime = m * current_p_val
            is_pairwise_coprime = True
            for j in range(i):
                if not is_coprime(candidate_p_i_prime, T_perp_c[j].p):
                    is_pairwise_coprime = False
                    break
            if is_pairwise_coprime:
                p_i_prime = candidate_p_i_prime
                break
            m += 1
        T_perp_c.append(SporadicTask(e_i_prime, d_i_prime, p_i_prime))
    return T_perp_c
key_insights: This transformation is a core part of the first reduction, ensuring that the transformed task set retains schedulability properties while gaining the pairwise coprime period property.

formal_description.statement: hat_lambda is the smallest number such that hat_lambda equiv d_i (mod p_i) for all (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T_perp_c AND hat_lambda > max{p_i | (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T_perp_c}.
assumptions: Tasks in T_perp_c have pairwise coprime periods.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific time point hat_lambda, found using the Chinese Remainder Theorem, which satisfies certain congruence and magnitude conditions.

informal_sketch.intuition: hat_lambda is a special time instant where, for every task in `T_perp_c`, the time `hat_lambda` has the same remainder as the task's deadline `d_i` when divided by its period `p_i`. This means that at `hat_lambda`, all tasks 'align' in a specific way relative to their deadlines and periods. The pairwise coprimality of periods guarantees such a `hat_lambda` exists and can be found efficiently.
steps: For each task `tau_i` in `T_perp_c`, we need `hat_lambda % p_i == d_i % p_i` (or `hat_lambda == d_i` if `d_i < p_i`).
Since `T_perp_c` has pairwise coprime periods, the Chinese Remainder Theorem can be used to find a solution for `hat_lambda` that satisfies all these congruences.
Find the smallest such `hat_lambda` that is also greater than the maximum period in `T_perp_c`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def find_hat_lambda(T_perp_c):
    # This requires an implementation of the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)
    # and finding the smallest solution greater than max_p.
    # For example, using a library or custom CRT function:
    congruences = [] # List of (remainder, modulus) pairs
    max_p = 0
    for task in T_perp_c:
        congruences.append((task.d % task.p, task.p))
        if task.p > max_p:
            max_p = task.p

    # hat_lambda = solve_crt(congruences)
    # while hat_lambda <= max_p:
    #     hat_lambda += product_of_all_moduli # CRT solutions repeat with this period
    # return hat_lambda
    pass
key_insights: hat_lambda is a critical point for the second reduction, allowing a duality between EDF's demand bound function and FP's request bound function to be established.

dependencies: Definition 20: T_perp_c and its task parameters

formal_description.statement: T_FP def = T_hp_FP union {tau_low}, where T_hp_FP def = {(e_i, p_i, p_i) | (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T_perp_c} and tau_low def = (e_low, d_low, p_low) with e_low def = hat_lambda - dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda + 1, d_low def = hat_lambda, and p_low def = phi * hat_lambda for some positive integer phi.

variables.T_FP: the final task set for FP schedulability analysis
variables.T_hp_FP: set of higher-priority tasks in T_FP
variables.e_i: execution time of task i from T_perp_c
variables.p_i: period of task i from T_perp_c
variables.d_i: deadline of task i from T_perp_c
variables.dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda: demand bound function of T_perp_c at hat_lambda (Definition 15)

assumptions: T_perp_c is a task set with pairwise coprime periods (Definition 20).
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the task set T_FP, constructed for the FP-schedulability problem, consisting of higher-priority tasks derived from T_perp_c and a specially constructed lowest-priority task tau_low.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the final task set constructed for the NP-hardness proof. It's designed such that its FP-schedulability is directly linked to the EDF-schedulability of the original `T_perp_c`. It consists of two parts: a set of higher-priority tasks (`T_hp_FP`) which are essentially `T_perp_c` tasks with implicit deadlines, and a single, carefully crafted lowest-priority task (`tau_low`) whose schedulability determines the schedulability of the entire `T_FP` set.
steps: Create `T_hp_FP`: For each task `(e_i, d_i, p_i)` in `T_perp_c`, create a new task `(e_i, p_i, p_i)`. This makes them implicit-deadline tasks.
Create `tau_low = (e_low, d_low, p_low)`:
`d_low = hat_lambda`.
`e_low = hat_lambda - dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda + 1` (this value is chosen to create the desired duality).
`p_low = phi * hat_lambda` (phi is chosen to satisfy implicit or constrained deadline conditions for `tau_low`).
Combine `T_hp_FP` and `tau_low` to form `T_FP`.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def create_T_FP(T_perp_c, hat_lambda, dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda, phi):
    T_hp_FP = []
    for task in T_perp_c:
        T_hp_FP.append(SporadicTask(task.e, task.p, task.p)) # Implicit deadlines

    e_low = hat_lambda - dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda + 1
    d_low = hat_lambda
    p_low = phi * hat_lambda
    tau_low = SporadicTask(e_low, d_low, p_low)

    T_FP = T_hp_FP + [tau_low]
    return T_FP, tau_low
key_insights: The construction of `tau_low` is central to the reduction, as its parameters are specifically chosen to invert the EDF-schedulability condition of `T_perp_c` into an FP-schedulability condition for `T_FP`.

results.identifier: Theorem I.1: Equivalence of Sporadic and Synchronous Periodic Tasks

formal_description.statement: Let T be a set of sporadic tasks, and let T_prime be a set of synchronous periodic tasks with the same parameters as the tasks in T. Then, on a preemptive uniprocessor (i) T is FP-schedulable with a given priority ordering if and only if T_prime is FP-schedulable with the same priority ordering, and (ii) T is EDF-schedulable if and only if T_prime is EDF-schedulable.

variables.T_prime: a set of synchronous periodic tasks with identical parameters

formal_description.conclusion: The choice between sporadic and synchronous periodic task models does not affect FP or EDF schedulability on a preemptive uniprocessor.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem simplifies analysis by stating that for FP and EDF on a single processor, we can treat sporadic tasks as synchronous periodic tasks (or vice-versa) without changing the schedulability outcome. This is because the worst-case scenario for sporadic tasks (all jobs arriving as early as possible) mimics synchronous periodic tasks.
steps: Consider a task set T of sporadic tasks.
Create a corresponding task set T_prime of synchronous periodic tasks, where each task in T_prime has the same (e, d, p) parameters as its counterpart in T.
If T is FP-schedulable, then T_prime is also FP-schedulable with the same priority order, and vice-versa.
If T is EDF-schedulable, then T_prime is also EDF-schedulable, and vice-versa.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_equivalence(sporadic_T, periodic_T_prime, scheduler_type, priority_order=None):
    # This theorem is a theoretical equivalence, not a direct algorithm.
    # It implies that if is_fp_schedulable(sporadic_T, priority_order) is True,
    # then is_fp_schedulable(periodic_T_prime, priority_order) is also True.
    # And similarly for EDF.
    pass
key_insights: This equivalence allows researchers to use the simpler synchronous periodic model for worst-case analysis, as it covers the most demanding scenarios for sporadic tasks.

assumptions: Task set T has constrained deadlines (Definition 4).
formal_description.conclusion: DM priority ordering (Definition 11) is an optimal priority assignment for constrained-deadline task sets under FP scheduling.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is very powerful: it means that when dealing with constrained-deadline tasks under FP scheduling, we don't need to search for the 'best' priority assignment. If a task set can be scheduled by *any* fixed-priority scheme, it can also be scheduled by simply assigning priorities based on deadlines (DM).

If there exists *any* priority ordering `P_any` for which `is_fp_schedulable(T, P_any)` is True.
Then, if we apply `assign_dm_priorities(T)` to get `P_DM`.
It must be that `is_fp_schedulable(T, P_DM)` is also True.

    # It implies that to check FP-schedulability for constrained deadlines,
    # one only needs to check with DM priority ordering.
    # If is_fp_schedulable(task_set, assign_dm_priorities(task_set)) is True,
    # then it's schedulable. If False, it's unschedulable by any FP scheme.

key_insights: DM optimality significantly reduces the search space for finding a schedulable priority assignment for constrained-deadline systems.

results.identifier: Theorem I.3: Liu and Layland Utilization Bound for RM/Implicit Deadlines

formal_description.statement: A task set T of n implicit-deadline tasks is FP-schedulable on a preemptive uniprocessor with the RM priority ordering if U_T <= n * (2_power_1_div_n - 1). Note that lim n->infinity n * (2_power_1_div_n - 1) = ln 2 approx 0.693, which leads to the simpler sufficient condition U_T <= ln_2.
assumptions: Task set T has implicit deadlines (Definition 3).
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a sufficient condition for FP-schedulability of implicit-deadline tasks under RM priority ordering based on utilization.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a classic result: if the total utilization of a set of implicit-deadline tasks is below a certain threshold (which depends on the number of tasks, or approximately 69.3% for many tasks), then the tasks are guaranteed to be schedulable using Rate-Monotonic priority assignment. It's a quick check, but only a sufficient condition (meaning tasks might still be schedulable even if they exceed this bound).
steps: Calculate the total utilization `U_T` for the task set `T` (Definition 13).
Count the number of tasks `n` in `T`.
Calculate the Liu and Layland bound: `n * (2^(1/n) - 1)`.
If `U_T` is less than or equal to this bound, the task set is FP-schedulable with RM.
A simpler, more conservative check is `U_T <= ln_2` (approx 0.693).
key_insights: This theorem provides a simple, fast, but conservative test for schedulability in a common scenario. It was one of the first major results in real-time scheduling theory.

results.identifier: Theorem I.4: Joseph and Pandya Response Time Analysis for FP

formal_description.statement: Let tau_low = (e_low, d_low, p_low) be a constrained-deadline task scheduled by the FP scheduler on a preemptive uniprocessor, and let T_hp be the set of tasks with higher priority than tau_low in the given priority ordering. The response time r_low of tau_low is then the smallest positive fixed point to r_low = e_low + rbf_T_hp_r_low. All jobs generated by tau_low are guaranteed to meet their deadlines with the given priority ordering if and only if r_low <= d_low.

variables.T_hp: set of tasks with higher priority than tau_low
variables.rbf_T_hp_r_low: request bound function for T_hp in interval r_low (Definition 14)

formal_description.conclusion: Provides an exact condition for FP-schedulability of a task by calculating its worst-case response time.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem provides an exact way to determine if a task will meet its deadline under FP scheduling. It calculates the worst-case time a task might take to complete (its response time) by considering its own execution time plus all the interference it receives from higher-priority tasks. If this response time is less than or equal to its deadline, the task is schedulable.
steps: For a task `tau_low`, identify all tasks `T_hp` that have higher priority.
Solve the equation `r_low = e_low + rbf(T_hp, r_low)` iteratively to find the smallest positive fixed point for `r_low`.
Start with `r_low_0 = e_low`.
Iterate `r_low_k+1 = e_low + rbf(T_hp, r_low_k)` until `r_low_k+1 = r_low_k` or `r_low_k+1 > d_low`.
If a fixed point `r_low` is found and `r_low <= d_low`, then `tau_low` is schedulable.
key_insights: Response time analysis is the most common and accurate method for FP schedulability, especially for constrained deadlines. It accounts for preemption and interference directly.

results.identifier: Theorem I.5: Baruah et al. EDF-Schedulability Condition

formal_description.statement: A task set T is EDF-schedulable on a preemptive uniprocessor if and only if U_T <= 1 and forall lambda >= 0, dbf_T_lambda <= lambda.

variables.dbf_T_lambda: demand bound function of T in interval lambda (Definition 15)

formal_description.conclusion: Provides an exact condition for EDF-schedulability for task sets with arbitrary deadlines.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem provides a necessary and sufficient condition for EDF schedulability. It states that two conditions must hold: first, the total processor utilization cannot exceed 100%, and second, for any time interval length, the total demand for execution time by jobs whose deadlines fall within that interval must not exceed the interval's length. If both hold, EDF can schedule the tasks.
steps: Calculate the total utilization `U_T` (Definition 13). If `U_T > 1`, the task set is unschedulable.
For all possible interval lengths `lambda` (from 0 up to a certain bound, or indefinitely for arbitrary deadlines):
Calculate `dbf(T, lambda)` (Definition 15).
If `dbf(T, lambda) > lambda` for any `lambda`, the task set is unschedulable.
If both conditions hold, the task set is EDF-schedulable.
key_insights: This is a powerful and exact schedulability test for EDF, applicable to all deadline types. The challenge lies in checking 'all lambda >= 0', which often requires bounding the search space.

results.identifier: Corollary I.6: EDF-Schedulability for Constrained Deadlines over Hyper-period

formal_description.statement: A task set T with constrained deadlines is EDF-schedulable on a preemptive uniprocessor if and only if U_T <= 1 and forall lambda in {0, 1, ..., P_T - 1}, dbf_T_lambda <= lambda.

variables.dbf_T_lambda: demand bound function of T in interval lambda (Definition 15)

assumptions: Task set T has constrained deadlines (Definition 4).
formal_description.conclusion: Simplifies the EDF-schedulability check for constrained-deadline task sets by limiting the interval lengths to be checked up to the hyper-period.

informal_sketch.intuition: This corollary is a practical extension of Theorem I.5 for constrained-deadline tasks. It states that if tasks have constrained deadlines, we don't need to check the demand bound function for *all* `lambda >= 0`. We only need to check up to the hyper-period `P_T`, because the demand pattern repeats after this interval, and critical instants for constrained deadlines occur within this range.
steps: Calculate the total utilization `U_T` (Definition 13). If `U_T > 1`, the task set is unschedulable.
Calculate the hyper-period `P_T` (Definition 16).
For all integer interval lengths `lambda` from 0 up to `P_T - 1`:
Calculate `dbf(T, lambda)` (Definition 15).
If `dbf(T, lambda) > lambda` for any `lambda` in this range, the task set is unschedulable.
If both conditions hold, the task set is EDF-schedulable.
key_insights: This corollary makes EDF schedulability analysis for constrained deadlines computationally feasible, as the search space for `lambda` becomes finite (though potentially large).

results.identifier: Theorem I.7: Hardness of EDF-Schedulability with Bounded Utilization

formal_description.conclusion: The EDF-schedulability problem is computationally hard (coNP-complete) even under significant restrictions.

This hardness result is the starting point for the reductions in this paper.

results.identifier: Lemma II.1: EDF-Schedulability Equivalence under Scaling and Period Perturbation

formal_description.statement: Let T be a task set with constrained deadlines and let T_prime be another task set satisfying T_prime = {(k * e_i, k * d_i, k * p_i + delta_i) | (e_i, d_i, p_i) in T}, where k is a positive integer and 0 <= delta_i < k * p_i / P_T. Then, T_prime is EDF-schedulable if and only if T is EDF-schedulable.

variables.T: original task set with constrained deadlines
variables.e_i: execution time of task i in T
variables.d_i: relative deadline of task i in T
variables.p_i: period of task i in T
variables.delta_i: a small non-negative integer perturbation for period i

formal_description.conclusion: Scaling task parameters and slightly perturbing periods (within a bound related to the hyper-period) does not change the EDF-schedulability of a task set.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma is crucial for the first reduction. It says that if you scale all task parameters (execution times, deadlines, periods) by a common factor 'k' and then slightly adjust the periods (by `delta_i`) within a small bound, the EDF schedulability of the system remains unchanged. This allows for the construction of `T_perp_c` with coprime periods without altering its fundamental schedulability.

Show that `dbf(T_prime, lambda) <= k * dbf(T, lambda/k)`.
Since `dbf(T, lambda/k) <= lambda/k`, it follows that `dbf(T_prime, lambda) <= k * (lambda/k) = lambda`.
Thus, T_prime is EDF-schedulable.
**Part 2: T_prime is EDF-schedulable => T is EDF-schedulable**

Show that `dbf(T, lambda) <= dbf(T_prime, k * lambda + P_T) / k`.
Since `dbf(T_prime, k * lambda + P_T) <= k * lambda + P_T`, it follows that `dbf(T, lambda) <= (k * lambda + P_T) / k = lambda + P_T/k`.

Using Corollary I.6, we only need to check `lambda` in `[0, P_T-1]`. For these `lambda`, `dbf(T, lambda) <= lambda + P_T/k` implies `dbf(T, lambda) <= lambda` because `dbf` is integer-valued and `P_T/k` is small enough.
Thus, T is EDF-schedulable.

formal_description.statement: T_perp_c is EDF-schedulable if and only if forall lambda in {0, 1, ..., hat_lambda}, dbf_T_perp_c_lambda <= lambda.

variables.dbf_T_perp_c_lambda: demand bound function of T_perp_c at lambda (Definition 15)

assumptions: T_perp_c is a task set with constrained deadlines and pairwise coprime periods.
formal_description.conclusion: For task sets with pairwise coprime periods and bounded utilization, EDF-schedulability can be checked by examining the demand bound function only up to hat_lambda.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma refines the EDF schedulability test (Theorem I.5) for the specific task set `T_perp_c`. Because `T_perp_c` has pairwise coprime periods and its utilization is bounded, and given the special properties of `hat_lambda`, it's sufficient to check the demand bound function only up to `hat_lambda` (instead of the hyper-period or infinity). This significantly limits the search space for counterexamples to EDF schedulability.

**Sufficiency:** Assume `dbf(T_perp_c, lambda) <= lambda` for `lambda` in `[0, hat_lambda]`, but `T_perp_c` is *not* EDF-schedulable.
By Theorem I.5, there must exist some `lambda_prime > hat_lambda` where `dbf(T_perp_c, lambda_prime) > lambda_prime`.

Using the properties of `dbf` and the fact that `hat_lambda` satisfies `hat_lambda equiv d_i (mod p_i)`, it can be shown that such a `lambda_prime` cannot exist if the condition holds up to `hat_lambda` and `U_T_perp_c < 1`.

The proof uses the property `dbf(T_perp_c, hat_lambda + lambda) >= dbf(T_perp_c, hat_lambda) + lambda * U(T_perp_c)` and the assumption `dbf(T_perp_c, hat_lambda) <= hat_lambda` to show a contradiction.
key_insights: This lemma provides a finite and relatively small interval (`[0, hat_lambda]`) to check for EDF schedulability, which is crucial for the polynomial-time nature of the reduction.

results.identifier: Lemma II.7: Duality between FP-schedulability of T_FP and EDF-unschedulability of T_perp_c

formal_description.statement: Task set T_FP is FP-schedulable with RM and DM priority ordering if and only if T_perp_c is not EDF-schedulable.

variables.rbf_T_hp_FP_r_low: request bound function for T_hp_FP in interval r_low (Definition 14)
variables.dbf_T_perp_c_lambda: demand bound function of T_perp_c at lambda (Definition 15)

assumptions: RM and DM priority orderings are used (Definitions 11, 12).
T_perp_c has constrained deadlines, pairwise coprime periods, and utilization bounded by c (0 < c <= ln_2).
formal_description.conclusion: Establishes a direct inverse relationship between the FP-schedulability of the constructed task set T_FP and the EDF-schedulability of the intermediate task set T_perp_c.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the core of the NP-hardness proof. It shows that the FP-schedulability of the specially constructed `T_FP` is exactly the opposite of the EDF-schedulability of `T_perp_c`. If `T_perp_c` is EDF-schedulable, `T_FP` is *not* FP-schedulable, and vice-versa. This 'duality' is achieved by carefully setting `e_low` and `d_low` based on `hat_lambda` and `dbf_T_perp_c_hat_lambda`.
steps: **Part 1: T_FP is FP-schedulable => T_perp_c is not EDF-schedulable**

Through algebraic manipulation, using the definitions of `e_low`, `d_low`, `rbf`, and `dbf`, it's shown that `dbf(T_perp_c, hat_lambda - r_low) = hat_lambda - r_low + 1`.
Let `lambda_prime = hat_lambda - r_low`. Then `dbf(T_perp_c, lambda_prime) = lambda_prime + 1`, which implies `dbf(T_perp_c, lambda_prime) > lambda_prime`.
By Theorem I.5 (or Lemma II.4), this means `T_perp_c` is not EDF-schedulable.
**Part 2: T_perp_c is not EDF-schedulable => T_FP is FP-schedulable**
Assume `T_perp_c` is not EDF-schedulable. By Lemma II.4, there exists some `lambda_prime` in `[0, hat_lambda]` such that `dbf(T_perp_c, lambda_prime) > lambda_prime`.
Let `r = d_low - lambda_prime = hat_lambda - lambda_prime`.
Through algebraic manipulation, it's shown that `r >= e_low + rbf(T_hp_FP, r)`.
This inequality, combined with `0 < e_low + rbf(T_hp_FP, 0)` (which is true since `e_low >= 1`), implies that there must exist a fixed point `r_low` for `tau_low` such that `0 < r_low <= r <= d_low`.
By Theorem I.4, `tau_low` is schedulable, and by Lemma II.6, `T_FP` is FP-schedulable.

    # (i.e., r_low <= d_low for tau_low) is equivalent to the negation
    # of the EDF-schedulability condition for T_perp_c (i.e., exists lambda s.t. dbf > lambda).
    # The specific construction of e_low and d_low is key to this duality.
    pass

formal_description.statement: Deciding whether a set of sporadic or synchronous periodic tasks is FP-schedulable with a given priority ordering on a preemptive uniprocessor is NP-hard in the weak sense. This holds even if restricted in either of the following ways: (i) All tasks have implicit deadlines and the priority ordering is RM. (ii) All tasks have constrained deadlines, the priority ordering is DM and the utilization of the task set is bounded from above by any constant c, such that 0 < c < 1.
formal_description.conclusion: The FP-schedulability problem is (weakly) NP-hard under various common restrictions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the main result of the paper. It proves that determining if a task set is FP-schedulable is computationally very difficult (NP-hard), even for simplified scenarios like implicit deadlines with RM priorities or constrained deadlines with DM priorities and low utilization. This means there's likely no efficient (polynomial-time) algorithm to solve this problem in general.
steps: The proof uses a polynomial-time many-one reduction from the EDF-schedulability problem (restricted to constrained deadlines, pairwise coprime periods, and utilization bounded by `c_prime`, where `0 < c_prime <= ln_2`), which is known to be coNP-complete by Lemma II.3.
The reduction constructs `T_FP` (Definition 22) from `T_perp_c` (Definition 20).
Lemma II.7 establishes that `T_FP` is FP-schedulable if and only if `T_perp_c` is *not* EDF-schedulable.
Since the source problem is coNP-complete, its complement (the problem of `T_perp_c` being *not* EDF-schedulable) is NP-complete.
Because `T_FP`'s FP-schedulability is equivalent to this NP-complete problem, FP-schedulability is NP-hard.
The two specific restrictions (i) and (ii) are achieved by setting the `phi` parameter (Definition 22) appropriately:

For (i) implicit deadlines/RM: Set `phi = 1`. This makes `p_low = hat_lambda = d_low`, so `tau_low` has implicit deadlines. `T_hp_FP` also has implicit deadlines. RM is optimal for implicit deadlines.

For (ii) constrained deadlines/DM/bounded utilization: Choose `c_prime = c/2` for the source EDF problem. Set `phi = 2/c`. This ensures `p_low = (2/c) * hat_lambda >= hat_lambda = d_low`, so `tau_low` has constrained deadlines. DM is optimal for constrained deadlines. The total utilization of `T_FP` is also shown to be bounded by `c`.
